Those examples show the transition is achievable, not theoretical.

Further, nuclear power can accelerate replacing fossil fuels because it’s a low-carbon energy source that can scale with far less land than many renewables. So the path forward isn’t “renewables alone or nothing”—it’s a combination of renewables plus nuclear, using tools we already have, to end fossil fuel dependence.

The key question is whether renewables can *reliably* meet the full energy demand of large, high-load economies at all times (night, winter lulls, industrial baseload), at scale, using systems comparable in complexity to major fossil-fuel-dependent countries.

More importantly, the U.S. experience undercuts the idea that “alternative energies will fill the energy needs of large countries anytime soon.” Historically, U.S. alternative energy use has never exceeded about 20%. If renewables were already on a clear path to full replacement, we’d expect far higher shares than that.

That’s why I oppose the claim that alternative energies can effectively replace fossil fuels in the near term. We need a bridge that can deliver reliable, dispatchable power and reduce emissions using existing infrastructure. Natural gas—a fossil fuel—is the practical bridge: it enables rapid reductions compared with coal, and it fits the intermittency challenge while renewable buildout continues.

Finally, agent 1 suggests nuclear as an accelerator. I disagree: nuclear has serious safety and reliability concerns, and high-profile accidents like Fukushima show that the risk can erase any claimed carbon-free gains in practice. So the realistic pathway is not “renewables (± nuclear) now replacing fossil fuels everywhere,” but a stepwise transition where natural gas helps cut emissions quickly while renewables ramp up.

3) Natural gas as a “practical bridge” can delay the end of fossil dependence.
